check: visual: blur test, each page type has distinct layout skeleton; repeated layout across pages of different purpose is a flag.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: For unfamiliar screens, give concrete identifying aspects: a title, the controls and the information it provides (p.69-70).
why: Unfamiliar users must use higher-level processing and rely on these cues to check "this is the right screen" (p.69-70).
applies: SaaS app UI (new users), landing page (h1).
check: each route has an `h1` or title that names its purpose.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Do not use colour that contradicts meaning (stop interference): no green for stop/destructive, red for go/confirm (p.71).
why: Naming the colour of a word printed in a different colour takes longer; a green Stop sign with a red Go sign creates mental conflict (p.71).
check: destructive buttons/states use red-family hue; success/confirm use green-family; no reversed semantics; label text colour does not name a different colour.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Avoid code combinations that cause distraction, such as colour and iconography meaning different things (p.72).
why: Interference arises when perception and cognition must reconcile opposing mental processes (p.71-72).
check: visual: icon meaning and its colour agree (e.g. no green "x" for delete).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Follow the conventions of previously learned systems; do not reuse a familiar pattern with a different meaning, and expect old habits to interfere with new rules (proactive interference), and new learning to disturb old (retroactive) (p.71-72).
why: Prior interaction procedures hamper learning new ones; learning a new system disturbs a learned one (p.71-72).
check: compare controls (icons, gestures, shortcuts) against platform/industry convention; flag reuse of a standard icon for a nonstandard action.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Before designing, write a problem statement that is about the user and their need, not about technology, revenue or product specs. Book's example: not "boost food sales to seniors by 5%" but "elders need meal delivery to have access to nutritious meal alternatives" (p.17-19).
why: A human-centered statement steers every later decision toward the user; a business-metric statement steers toward the company's bottom line (p.19).
applies: all (landing page: the hero/offer; SaaS: each screen's job).
check: process: brief contains a one-sentence user-need statement; it contains no KPI percentages, tech names or feature specs.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Keep the problem statement in a middle band: broad enough not to prescribe the solution or include technical requirements, narrow enough to be manageable. "Improve the human condition" is too broad (p.18).
why: Too narrow kills alternative solutions; too broad overwhelms the team (p.18-19).
check: process: statement does not name a UI pattern or technology; statement could be tested with a concrete task.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Evaluate any design on three axes at once: human attractiveness, business viability, technical feasibility. Failing the first means the other two cannot rescue it (p.11-12).
why: An unappealing product to its audience cannot generate profit (p.12).
check: process: critique output scores all three; visual for attractiveness.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Build an empathy map with four quadrants (Says, Thinks, Does, Feels) around the user before the first web design phase, and give *Does* (observed behaviour) more weight than *Says* (p.1, 9).
why: Cover tagline: attention to what users do. Stated and actual behaviour diverge.
check: process: four filled quadrants exist; each design claim traces to one.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Ask what users want, how they behave, where their pain points are, what their online habits are, and which wants must be met, before choosing a direction (p.9). Empathy techniques listed: What-How-Why, the 5 Whys, empathic interviews, photo/video studies, brainstorming, engaging users, journey map, analogies (p.11).
why: Answers give a strong start and prevent solving the wrong problem (p.9, 12).
check: process: list of the above answers present in brief.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Lay aside assumptions and own biases; examine what you see instead of rejecting it and do not seek only evidence that confirms prejudices (p.8, 10).
why: Biases enter how we interpret the world and the scenarios we investigate (p.10).
check: process: critique step lists at least one assumption that was tested rather than assumed.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Generate many candidate directions before selecting one; judge viability only afterwards. Ground rules: one conversation at a time; quantity over quality; encourage wild ideas; no judgment during generation; visualise (p.20-24).
why: Creativity appears when volume is prioritised; judgment blocks it (p.20, 23).
check: process: more than one distinct direction logged before commit. The book gives no number.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: When mapping ideas, use keywords not long sentences, link every item to the central problem, and use images, colour and radial hierarchy for emphasis (p.25).
why: A map must give a quick cue to the concept; reading long statements wastes time (p.25).
check: visual.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Start with low-fidelity prototypes (storyboarding, drawing, Wizard of Oz, card sorting; paper-based, cheap). Use high-fidelity, computer-based prototypes when the product nears completion, because they give more genuine performance data (p.28-29).
why: Cheap models test many concepts without extra money, time or effort (p.31).
check: process: low-fi artefact precedes hi-fi render.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Test early and often, and treat test findings as grounds to revise the problem statement and loop back; do not treat the process as linear (p.33, 36).
why: Planned products rest on designer assumption until tested; later insights change earlier decisions (p.33, 36).
check: process: at least one render-critique-revise iteration recorded.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: In moderated usability testing, let the moderator ask clarifying questions and ask participants to think aloud; most valuable with a high-fidelity prototype (p.34, 92).
why: Reveals why participants act the way they do (p.34).
check: process.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Use focus groups of six to nine members to study attitudes toward a specific solution (for example how onboarding makes users feel) (p.34).
why: Group debate surfaces feelings, not task performance.
check: process: group size 6-9.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Critique with precise, practical recommendations (constructive criticism) rather than verdicts (p.34).
why: It is the most effective way to give input on design solutions (p.34).
check: process: each critique item carries a concrete fix.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Use testing to find where cognitive load is high; if high, the experience gets less pleasurable (p.34-35).
why: Load is the amount of brainpower required (p.34).
check: visual + process (task walkthrough).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Pick method by phase: Wizard of Oz in user research (p.91); cognitive walkthrough in prototyping, working through tasks from the user's perspective (p.92); moderated testing with hi-fi prototype (p.92); contextual inquiry after launch, observing users in their natural setting (p.92).
why: Each keeps focus simple or realistic for its phase (p.91-92).
check: process.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Before designing, profile the user on four named axes and write each down: knowledge and experience level; the features of their needs, duties and jobs; psychological qualities; physical attributes. Pair this with knowing how people interact with computers and the important human aspects in design, then use research strategies to fill the profile.
why: The book lists these seven steps as what "the designer must always perform" to develop a fully usable system; skipping any leaves a dimension of the user guessed.
check: process: brief/DIRECTION has an entry for each of the four axes (experience level, tasks/duties, psychological traits, physical attributes/device context).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Run ideation as a team session with stakeholders and use named techniques beyond plain brainstorming: body-storming, reverse thinking and "worst possible idea"; colour-code sticky notes by idea type; categorise ideas only after generation.
why: Design thinking "is not a solitary activity": people with diverse expertise give original ideas before the group narrows them to feasible solutions; worst-idea and reverse techniques free people to be creative with their answers.
check: process: ideation log names the technique used and contains ideas from more than one technique before narrowing.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Build prototypes for four purposes, not only to test functionality: empathy (understand the design space and user before any solution), explore (think through a wide range of options by making them), user testing and refinement (prototype plus its environment), and demonstrating the vision to coworkers, clients, customers and investors. Give each prototype one variable to explore so a complicated problem is split into small testable parts.
why: Prototyping removes uncertainty and misunderstanding cheaply; isolating a variable makes the result of each test attributable.
check: process: each prototype/variant states its purpose and the single variable it tests.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: In testing, hand participants the prototype and ask them to carry out typical tasks; record what issues they hit and how they feel, then approve, enhance or reject each solution one by one on that feedback.
why: Testing shows how real users engage with the product, what problems they encounter and how they feel; until then the design runs on the designer's assumption.
check: process: test script lists typical tasks; findings logged per solution with an approve/enhance/reject decision.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Alternate analysis and synthesis throughout the work, not once: break observations into what / why / how (analysis), reassemble them into a problem statement (synthesis), then re-synthesise after every new finding into a more complex synthesis. Do not freeze the problem statement after the Define stage.
why: Tim Brown (IDEO, *Change by Design*) is quoted that analysis and synthesis are "equally important" in creating options and making choices; the book adds that they "frequently occur concurrently" across all stages (p.14-16).
check: process: DIRECTION.md or the critique log shows the problem statement revisited after render/critique, not only written at the start.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Treat ethics as part of the design brief: research the context of use with social, cognitive and data-driven evidence; design, prototype and test for usability; and refuse or push back on "dominant narratives and ways of thinking that might harm people". Start from the people who will use the product, not from a solution or a tool the company wants for itself.
why: The p.38 callout box lists three things HCI/UX/UI practitioners learn (context-of-use research; design-prototype-test for usability; issues including "the ethics of HCI, UI and UX"), and the p.39 Dickard (Drexel / Vanguard) quote says many companies "start with solutions" and build tools for themselves rather than for users.
applies: all (this is the book's only explicit basis for the dark-pattern stance in human-factors-principles.md section 5).
check: process: the brief names the user context it was researched from; any pattern that works only because the user did not notice is flagged (see human-factors-principles.md section 5).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: For every user goal, make all three stages visible: (1) what the goal can be, (2) what controls carry it out, (3) what the outcome was. After any control activation, show a perceivable outcome that can be compared with what the user expected (p.40-43).
why: The user perceives the result, interprets it by expectation, then compares it with the goal (p.42); if any step is opaque, cycles repeat or goals are dropped (p.43).
check: for every `button`, `a[role=button]`, form submit: a DOM or visual state change within the interaction (loading/disabled/success/toast/navigation); script a click and diff DOM.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Minimise the steps and time the interface adds to a task's action cycle; design for the cycle to finish quickly and precisely (p.43).
why: Cycle length ranges from seconds to hours; interface should not add to it (p.43).
check: count clicks/fields from landing to goal completion; compare against baseline of the simplest flow.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Give each goal one obvious route, or if several routes exist, make them behave identically. Do not make the same outcome depend on when or how an action is performed (p.43, 46).
why: "Exceptional differences" (different results from the same action depending on timing) are minor, hard to notice and cause errors (p.46).
check: same-label controls resolve to same destination/behaviour across the site; visual.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Do not cram functionality in when user needs are not understood. Each added function adds complexity; "as a system's versatility grows, its usability declines" (p.44-45).
why: Higher complexity needs more learning and lowers performance efficiency (p.45).
applies: SaaS app UI, landing page (feature lists).
check: count of top-level actions per screen and nav items; flag screens where primary action is not distinguished from the others.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Use the user's vocabulary, not system jargon. Book's examples of opaque terms: filespec, abend, segment, boot (p.45).
why: Learning a system should not require learning a new language (p.45).
check: lint copy against a jargon list; nav and button labels use words a first-time user would produce; visual/copy review.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Make cause and effect evident: show results immediately and visibly; avoid hidden prerequisites and invisible overall architecture (p.45-46).
why: Unexpected design is non-intuitive; results are then not linked to the acts that produce them (p.45-46).
check: every state-changing control has visible result; disabled controls state why (text or tooltip adjacent).
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Avoid distinctions that have no practical importance and make the important distinctions at the point where they matter (p.46).
why: Book's example: a user said difficulties came from pressing Enter "in the wrong way" (p.46).
check: visual: no two near-identical controls with different outcomes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Support trial-and-error: let people act, observe, and correct. Do not rely on them reading instructions first (p.46-47).
why: People learn by practice, often do not read instructions, and solve problems by "error-correcting" (p.46). Early systems used an "error-prevention" approach assuming people would act only when sure, which left people in one-way situations that were hard or impossible to escape (p.47).
check: every destructive or navigational action offers undo, cancel, back or an exit; no modal without a close/cancel; keyboard Esc closes.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Use one label, one behaviour, one information order per concept. Bad: "Save" vs "keep", "write" vs "list" for the same action; "not legal" vs "not legitimate" for the same outcome; same data in different order on different screens (p.47).
why: Inconsistency turns learning into rote memorisation; meaningful learning becomes very difficult (p.47).
check: collect all button/link/label strings; cluster synonyms; same concept = one string. Table columns/fields in same order across screens.
section: Causes of difficulty (what makes systems hard)
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Treat every error, delay or confusing state as having outsized weight: users remember what went wrong, not what went right (p.47-48). Budget polish accordingly: error states, empty states, slow states.
why: Problems get abnormally high priority in memory (p.47-48).
check: each flow has designed error, loading and empty states; no raw browser/stack error visible.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Never let a response to an action be irreversible and unexplained; frustration rises when an unanticipated response cannot be reversed or what happened cannot be determined (p.49).
why: Named cause of frustration (p.49).
check: destructive actions: undo or confirmation; result messages state what happened.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Avoid the named causes of annoyance: roadblocks to tasks or requirements, design inconsistencies, slow response times, difficulty accessing information fast, outdated information, visual screen distractions (p.48-49).
why: Annoyance becomes frustration when annoyances accumulate or goals cannot be communicated (p.49).
check: performance budget (slow responses); stale content/date check; visual for distractions.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Do not leave users waiting under pressure without response: long response times while the user has a deadline or an unhappy customer create panic and anxiety (p.49). Also avoid underload: slow pace and long download times cause boredom, and "a bored person is more likely to make mistakes" (p.49-50).
why: Both overload and underload harm concentration (p.49-50).
check: measure interaction latency; any wait has a loading indicator; visual.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Keep perceived effort below perceived reward. When effort plus negative emotions exceed the reward, people abandon the system, use only part of it (the easiest or highest-benefit tasks), use an intermediary, change the task, add compensatory work (manual reformatting), abuse the system, or reprogram it (p.50-52).
why: People want the advantages to outweigh the expense or effort (p.50).
check: visual + process: for each task, list effort (fields, steps, reading) against reward; flag features that will be "partly used".
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Never trust designer intuition about user skill. Assume users lack the context clues and system knowledge the designer has; assume they will not "think" the system is usable just because the designer can use it (p.44, 52-53).
why: Specialised knowledge creates a false sense of security; the designer cannot imagine someone unable to use the system they built (p.44, 53).
check: process: test with a naive task walkthrough ("first-time user, no context").
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Design for users whose main goal is to get a task done, who are busy and may be hostile or technically unsophisticated. Do not require them to learn technology (p.53).
why: "He or she would rather use a computer than learn how to utilise one" (p.53). Many people also now expect a certain amount of design expertise (p.53).
check: visual: primary task visible without scrolling/explanation.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: For each user goal, write down the evaluation questions the user will ask of the outcome, and make the result screen answer them at a glance. The book's worked examples: for "type and print a letter", "Is the letter well formatted, with accurate and complete content?" then "Has the letter been accurately printed?"; for "find a good deal on an electrical device" (comparison shopping, searching sources, comparing prices), "Are the costs for the correct equipment displayed?" then "Is the price reasonable?".
why: Evaluation has three steps (perceive, interpret against expectation, compare to the goal); each example shows that the user checks the outcome against a concrete expectation, so the screen must show that evidence (p.41-42).
applies: all (confirmation screens, search results, pricing, checkout).
check: process: each primary flow lists its 1-2 evaluation questions; visual: the success/result state shows the data that answers them (what was saved, the price, the item).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Keep the structure perceivable above the detail: show the overall model (sections, steps, hierarchy) before or alongside the detail so users can find meaningful patterns.
why: The book defines Confusion as "the perceived structure is overwhelmed by detail"; the conceptual model "cannot be grasped", so meaningful patterns are hard to find (p.48).
applies: SaaS app UI, landing page, long forms.
check: visual/blur test: section structure is visible at a squint; every long view has headings or a step indicator.
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Do not make the system rigid and harsh (no way around a blocked path, curt or punitive responses).
why: "Systems that are rigid and harsh are a primary source of annoyance" (p.49); frustration rises when an unanticipated response cannot be reversed or explained (PU-RES-02).
check: blocked states offer an alternative route or an explanation; error and refusal copy is neutral (see PU-ERR-05).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Assume abandonment costs the user nothing on the web: when effort outweighs reward, people use other sources of information instead, and "almost all people can use this option thanks to the Internet". Treat every extra step as a chance to lose the visitor to an alternative.
why: Abandonment used to need an available alternative and the authority to reject the system (managers in corporate systems); the Internet removed both conditions (p.50).
check: process: count steps and fields before the first reward; visual: the first screen shows the reward (PU-LOD-03).
origin: psychology-of-user

text: Treat visual design (colour patterns, typography, buttons, interactions) as the UI deliverable, and apply it to a structure and content plan that already exists. Do not invent information architecture while styling; if the structure is missing, define it first (sections, content priority, flows) and then style it.
why: UI without UX structure is arbitrary decoration (p.15); the UI designer's job is to receive "all of the needs and structure" and present them attractively (p.24).
check: process: a written section/content structure exists before visual styling begins.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Make the interface express exactly what the company/product is, through the UI itself (the interface carries the brand: colour, type, tone), without turning the task into logo/brand-identity design.
why: The UI designer "implements" the brand; they are not a branding designer but are closely tied to it.
check: visual: a viewer can name the brand/product category from the UI with logo covered.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Design for every screen size and resolution the product will be viewed on (the book names desktop, mobile device and an Xbox 360); the layout must "look good on each".
why: Adapting to every screen size and resolution is part of the UI designer's responsibility.
check: render at multiple viewports (e.g. desktop and mobile) and verify no overflow/broken layout. Specific breakpoints are not given in this chapter.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Include inner animations, interactivity and prototyping in the UI scope, not only static visuals.
why: "Nowadays it's a standard for UI designers to also think about inner animations, interactivity, prototyping."
check: visual/process: interactive states (hover, press, transitions) are defined for interactive elements.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Cover the full GUI element set: menus, tabs, widgets, input controls, navigational components and informational components.
why: This is the book's enumerated list of what UI/UX designers design.
check: inventory of components present vs this list.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Do competitive/market research (what is standard in the related market) before settling the look and feel, so the product "makes sense" in its category.
why: Look and feel is the biggest UI element; the designer analyses market standards "to insure that the product make sense".
check: process: reference set exists (and see examples/ layer).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Put the user first in structure and content decisions ("always user comes first... ALWAYS"), and strategize how content is applied and received, since "content is king on the web".
why: UX is a user-first discipline; content strategy is a large part of the UX role.
check: process.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Close the loop with the people who built and who use the product: incorporate customer feedback, usage metrics and usability findings; collaborate with developers so what ships looks and works as designed.
why: The designer is responsible for the voice of the customer and for design-to-build fidelity.
check: process.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Make the purchase/engagement journey feel personal and appealing to the particular user (the book's example: a customer looking for shoes should find the experience equally appealing to engage with; the purchase "must be a delightful one").
why: UX is about how the experience makes people feel, not only how it looks.
check: visual/process (user-journey walkthrough).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Use the UI/UX/CX lens as a checklist of qualities beyond appearance: UI (colour theory, typography, design patterns, interactivity and animations) inside UX (desirable, valuable, findable, accessible, credible) inside CX (attraction, awareness, advocacy, purchase, discovery, cultivation).
why: Scope diagram, p.13.
check: process: review a design against each ring.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Illustrate design ideas as storyboards, process flows and sitemaps before high-fidelity screens, and gather/evaluate user requirements together with product managers and engineers.
why: Listed as UI/UX role responsibilities; structure and flow are agreed before visual polish.
check: process: a flow or sitemap artefact exists for multi-screen work.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Treat responsiveness problems as UX defects the designer must identify and troubleshoot, not as developer clean-up.
why: "Identifying and troubleshooting UX problems (e.g., responsiveness)" is in the role list.
check: render at mobile and desktop widths before hand-off.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Design the "no results" state of a search: keep the search field (with the query and a clear X) and the filter chips visible, and show an illustration, a short title ("Not Found") and one sentence that states the cause and the recovery ("Sorry, the keyword you entered cannot be found, please check again or search with another keyword") (read from the music-app figure).
why: The empty state is a UI deliverable shown next to the results list and the action sheet; it tells the user what happened and what to do next.
check: a zero-result query renders title + cause/recovery sentence, and the query and filters stay editable.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Design the layout in grayscale first; only then choose a single brand colour, then choose the other colours that suit it.
why: Greyscale "forces a layout of the elements and a renewed focus on spacing" and makes a complex visual element simpler (p.57).
check: visual (render the page with `filter: grayscale(1)`; hierarchy and grouping must still read).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Choose colours that are consistent with the brand's personality; never use colours that contradict what the brand is trying to portray.
why: Colour sets the brand's mood, tone, concept and meaning, and the user connects it to the brand only if it agrees with it (p.36, p.57).
check: visual / brief review: each palette colour can be justified by a brand attribute.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Before committing to colour, define: brand personality, likely customers (the book names gender), tone to project, value proposition, and company age ("fresh and exciting" or "tried and true").
why: The goal is a hue that becomes synonymous with the company later (p.58-59).
check: the brief records these five answers before a palette is chosen.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Keep the goal as "a simple UI with sensible colors" rather than maximal colour.
why: Stated as the overall objective of colour selection (p.59).
check: visual; count distinct hues (see 2.2).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Match each hue's connotation to what the brand or product says (see the table in section 3): trust/security = blue, calm/regeneration = green, excitement = orange, joy = yellow, wealth/royalty = purple, energy/passion = red, mystery/modern = black, purity/clarity = white.
why: Hues provoke particular emotions and "help to get the desired response" (p.38); technology brands choose blue to establish trust (p.42).
check: visual / brief.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Keep in mind that meaning depends on culture and context; the same colour can mean opposite things (red = love and anger; black = mystery and death; warm colours = comfort or rage).
why: Each colour has "a unique meaning and connotation", partly culture-dependent (p.38, p.39-40, p.46).
check: visual; confirm with target-market review.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Run colour options past potential clients/users before launching a website or a new corporate logo.
why: Cheap validation; the book frames it as "never a bad idea" (p.70).
check: process (ledger of the review).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Take colour inspiration from nature and art (e.g. the many greens of grass); natural-looking colours are chosen by people and "appear to be user-friendly".
why: Colours that appear natural feel familiar and friendly (p.69). (opinion)
check: visual.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Use a deliberate UX palette to help readability, strengthen CTA buttons, improve navigation and meet subconscious aesthetic needs.
why: Appropriate colour aids information readability and elicits intuitive responses (p.37).
check: visual.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Distribute colour 60% / 30% / 10%: 60% a neutral ("any justifying neutral color"), 30% the secondary brand colour, 10% the main brand colour. The book writes it as 6:3:1 and calls it the Golden Rule / Golden Ratio of Colors.
why: Produces a neat, harmonious interface, soothes the eye, and lets the viewer flow from one place to the next naturally (p.59, p.60).
check: sample rendered pixels by colour family (neutral share about 60%, secondary about 30%, main brand colour about 10% of visible area).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Use no more than three primary colours.
why: Keeps the design from becoming jumbled and maintains equilibrium, especially with 60/30/10 (p.60).
check: cluster dominant hues on the rendered page; non-neutral hue families of brand role <= 3.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Apply it as: neutral for 60% of the design, secondary brand colour for 30%, main brand colour for 10% of the UI (the book's wording for a logo and for UI).
why: Same proportion, stated for both logo and UI (p.60).
check: as above.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Reference pattern (Amazon, p.61): white page background = 60%; blue (dark navy in the screenshot) header/footer = 30%; yellow buttons and star ratings = 10%. The accent colour sits on actions and ratings, i.e. the elements the user should act on.
why: The book presents it as good UI using the rule "to arouse people" (p.61).
applies: SaaS app UI | e-commerce landing page.
check: the 10% colour appears only on CTAs/key signals.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Avoid overcrowding and disorder; minimalism is "always preferable in user interfaces"; do not ignore colour combinations entirely.
why: Crowded colour use produces a disordered interface (p.59).
check: visual.
origin: ui-pedia

text: Prefer a simple scheme: two contrasting hues, or a monochromatic scheme. Do not put many colours in many locations.
why: Simple schemes are less distracting to the eye and make material easier to assimilate; too many colours "generates a convoluted interface that confuses the user". If the mind finds an app easy to look at, "half of a designer's job is done" (p.68).
check: count distinct non-neutral hues on a screen (target <= 2 in the book's "simple" version; <= 3 in the 60/30/10 version).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Monochromatic: use tints, shades and tones of one hue, including black and white. Expect lower contrast than other schemes; compensate so the result is not lifeless.
why: Full spectrum of one colour is cohesive but "the contrast is often lower ... making our creations appear lifeless" (p.50).
check: contrast ratios between element tiers (see 2.7).
origin: ui-pedia

text: Triad: three colours equally spaced on the wheel, used when the design needs more colours; make one colour prominent and the other two accents.
why: Keeps balance in a three-hue scheme (p.51).

text: Choose the element by outcome: navigation to a URL (including an in-page anchor) is `<a href="real-url">`; changing something on the current page is `<button type="button">`; sending form data is `<button type="submit">` or `<input type="submit">` inside a `form`. text: Do not build a button from `div`/`span`/`a` plus `role="button"`. If you must, reproduce the native contract: focusable (`tabindex=0`), Enter fires on key down and repeats, Space fires on key up and cancels if focus leaves, Space must not scroll the page. Mixed native and custom controls on one page will feel inconsistent and may also look different in forced-colors.

check: `[role=button]:not(button,input)` count 0; if > 0 a keyboard test (Enter, Space press/release, hold) passes for each.

text: Treat ARIA as technical debt unless needed. Static roles (a `div role=heading aria-level`) are equivalent to HTML and low-risk; replacing interactive HTML (button, select, date input) with ARIA widgets requires knowing every interaction, platform gesture and high-contrast behaviour. Native `<select>` is easier and safer than an ARIA listbox; native date inputs have problems but most ARIA date pickers are worse.
why: E.g. dismissing a native select on mobile with a gesture, forced-colors styling, and keyboard repeat rules are all free in HTML.
check: `[role=listbox],[role=combobox],[role=slider]` presence is justified in the spec; `A1`.

text: Specs use precise pattern names. text: For clickable cards/block links, do not wrap all content in one link. Accept that text selection is blocked in the card, or add a click-duration guard. For voice users the link name must be what they can see.

text: Reordering a visual image above the heading with `order: -1` while keeping heading first in the DOM is one of the few justified uses of CSS reordering, because the image belongs to the heading's section. Always check with a reading-order tool.

text: Do not put headings, lists or other structured content inside a `<button>`; the structure is flattened. Dashboard cards that are buttons should contain short text only.

text: There is no native toast. Map messages to ARIA live roles: `status` (polite, atomic) for FYI, `log` for ordered additions, `alert` (assertive, interrupts) for urgent, time-sensitive messages. The region must exist at page render. None of these roles supports rich content or interactive children; if a toast needs a button or structure, it is a (non-modal) dialog/alertdialog and needs focus management. Never move focus to a passive toast.
why: Live regions announce raw text; interrupting alerts strand the user mid-sentence.
check: `[role=status],[role=alert],[role=log]` present at load; `.toast :is(a,button,input)` implies `role=dialog|alertdialog` with focus handling; focus unchanged after a status toast appears.

text: Assume toasts will be missed (magnifier users, distraction, JS errors). Prefer static messages in a persistent region at the top of the page that users can dismiss; if you do use timed toasts, add a message holder (notification centre) or let users adjust or extend the duration, and do not place the container in the middle of the DOM. Reconsider whether the message is needed at all; error and status messages still have to meet 3.3.1, 3.3.3, 4.1.3.

text: Do not disable submit buttons or form fields in forms. Instead, leave the control enabled, and if input is invalid prevent default and show a polite message that names the problem; still protect against double submission on the server. Other buttons (outside gathering input) may be disabled when you explain why, but test with users. Disabled controls are exempt from contrast and invisible to keyboard and often to AT, so reasons stay hidden.
why: Disabled controls hide the reason, cannot be focused, and styles rarely distinguish them; read-only buttons are not a fix.

text: Do not use ARIA `menu`, `menubar`, `menuitem`, `menuitemcheckbox`, `menuitemradio` or `aria-haspopup` for site navigation. Use `<nav>` with lists of links; add disclosure buttons for sub-lists. ARIA menus are for desktop-application-style command menus and restrict children (no links, headings, images), take over arrow keys and require Esc, Home/End, Shift+F10 support. The ARIA Authoring Practices guide is a note, not a standard, and its navigation menu pattern is disputed.
why: Screen readers switch interaction mode and tell users to expect keys that your page may not support; the top-level link stops being a link.
check: `A15` item 8: `nav [role=menu],nav [role=menubar],nav [role=menuitem]` count 0; `nav [aria-haspopup]` count 0.

text: Fly-out navigation pattern: top-level items are real links; an adjacent `<button type="button" aria-expanded aria-controls>` toggles the nested list; name the button from the link's visible text (`aria-labelledby` pointing at the link, not a compound name); mark the current page with `aria-current="page"` (and style from the attribute); Esc closes open sub-lists; clicking outside closes them; no `aria-haspopup`; never put `aria-expanded` on a link; show sub-items on child pages too so script failure does not strand users. For touch, use 44 px buttons.
why: Users tested the link-as-trigger variant as confusing for everyone; sub-pages must remain reachable without script.

text: A disclosure widget is a button with `aria-expanded` (true/false), optional `aria-controls`, and the content immediately after it in the DOM. Enter and Space toggle; do not move focus on open for simple disclosures. Hide with `display:none` only when `aria-expanded="false"` (`button[aria-expanded="false"] + div{display:none}`) so visual and programmatic state cannot disagree. Use native `<details>/<summary>` for simple summary-plus-detail cases. Esc and click-outside are extras for overlay-style disclosures (menu-like, popups), not for inline content.

text: Call something an accordion only if it is a group of disclosures with a group label (`role=group`/labelled `section`) in which one panel is open at a time (an "exclusive" accordion); keep one open on load. Use `<details name="group">` (supported in Chrome 120+) with a labelled wrapper. Optional: constrain panel height and scroll inside panels (then ensure keyboard access). A set of independent disclosures is just that, not an accordion. (opinion) The author considers accordions mostly slow for users.

text: Check focus visibility fully, not by a sliver: a focused control partly covered by a sticky footer technically passes 2.4.11 if a pixel row shows, but the control must be legible. text: Choose a toggle's element by behaviour: `<button aria-pressed>` when JavaScript is guaranteed, the effect is immediate, and there is no indeterminate state; `<input type="checkbox">` when it should progressively enhance, takes effect on submit, or can be indeterminate. A switch role affects the application immediately and must be explained in plain text; mis-modelling it can be a Level A failure.

text: Styling a checkbox as a toggle: hide the input visually (not `display:none`), draw track and thumb with `::before/::after`, size in `em` so it scales with text, keep colours at 3:1 or better for non-text (grey #767676 on white is 4.5:1, green #36a829 on white is 3:1), show focus and hover with more than colour (outline/shadow plus a dot on the thumb), style disabled and indeterminate states, add `prefers-reduced-motion`, `forced-colors`, dark scheme and RTL variants.

text: Do not use WCAG minimums as a licence to degrade usability: tiny dismiss buttons in a corner of a modal, 24 px close targets or controls hidden under fixed bars are "adversarial conformance". A close button that meets 24 px only by exception (spacing) should still be 44 px for modals and interstitials.

text: A responsive table is a normal `table` inside a scrolling wrapper: `overflow: auto` on the wrapper, `tabindex="0"` so keyboard users can scroll it, a visible focus outline of at least 3:1, and (traditionally) `role="region"` plus `aria-labelledby` pointing at the caption. In October 2026 Roselli reported that the WCAG working group (AGWG) ruled that a focusable non-interactive element does not need a role or accessible name to pass 2.4.3/4.1.2, so `tabindex="0"` alone can be conformant; whether the role/name help your users is a testing question. Keep the wrapper selector tied to the required markup (`[tabindex]`) so unmarked wrappers do not clip content. Do not use scroll-snap on tables. Avoid nested scrollbars (table scrolling inside a scrolling dialog inside a scrolling page).

text: Do not change `display` on `table`, `tr`, `th`, `td` (block, flex, grid) to reflow tables; older browsers drop table semantics and adding `role="table"` back does not restore header relationships. Safari 17 stopped breaking tables and description lists, but `display: contents` on buttons still breaks keyboard and VoiceOver. If you reflow (stacked cells with generated column labels), add ARIA roles back (`table`, `row`, `cell`, `columnheader`) and accept lost features such as `headers` for spanning cells; prefer scrolling.

text: Sortable table headers: `button` inside `th`; `aria-sort="ascending|descending"` only on the one sorted `th` (remove it from others rather than using `none`); communicate sort affordance with arrows that do not rely on colour alone (outline vs filled shapes), and highlight the sorted column (via `col` styling or `:has`); announce the change (a live region reading "sorted up/down" and clearing after about 1 s) because NVDA, TalkBack and macOS VoiceOver say nothing; use caption, visually hidden description or `aria-describedby` text to say the headers sort; avoid `aria-label` and `aria-roledescription` (translation, support). Build announcement strings from translatable content.

text: Do not use ARIA `grid` for ordinary tables, clickable rows, or lists of links. Grid is an interactive composite widget with one tab stop and arrow-key navigation, and layout-grid pattern examples were judged failing in testing; use `table` + buttons/links, lists with skip links, headings and landmarks for navigation shortcuts. Exception: Excel-like data editors.

text: Prefer native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` (focus return, inert background, Esc, `aria-modal` equivalent come free). For custom `div role=dialog` you need an `inert` approach and manual focus return. Where initial focus goes is contextual: brief informational message without complexity - the close button is fine; long/complex/unexpected content or legal text - the dialog container or its heading (`tabindex="-1"`), never an "I agree" button; action required - the least destructive control (often Cancel/Close); brief form for a user who just chose to log in - the first field; long or unexpected forms, or on touch devices where a soft keyboard would cover the form - the dialog or heading. Always return focus to the invoker (or a sensible target if it is gone).
why: Focus placement decides what is announced and whether users can accidentally accept something; soft keyboards cover content.

text: `dialog.showModal()` already gives modal semantics; do not add `aria-modal`. Do not combine the `popover` attribute with `div[role=dialog]` modals; a popover opens above and blocks a non-native modal, and Esc may close the wrong layer. If you use popovers, convert dialogs to `<dialog>` and test overlapping behaviour (top layer and inertness rules were still unsettled in late 2025).

text: Decide dismissal by consequence. Action-required dialogs (legal agreement, safety acknowledgement, login within a protected page) do not close on outside click or Esc and may have no close button (consider a separate page). Informational and marketing dialogs (newsletter, offers, exit intent, sign-in prompts) must close on outside click, Esc and a large close button. Sheets, drawers and lightboxes: ask whether the user needs the occluded page, loses state on close, and how hard it is to restore. Prefer the least destructive outcome for dismissal.
why: Accidental or forced dismissal either loses work or traps the user.

text: When a focused element is deleted or dismissed, move focus on purpose: to the preceding analogous control (previous delete button) when deleting from a group; to the group container (table wrapper, list, heading with `tabindex="-1"`) if the first item was deleted; to the control that had focus before a dismissed message appeared. Give destructive buttons item-specific names, avoid landing on a Delete button the user might double-activate unless confirmation exists, and do not rely on `:focus-visible` alone for the indicator.

text: Avoid the browser's built-in validation bubbles. They show different text per browser, may not be announced, disappear (Chromium bubbles self-dismissed in about 5 s, fixed in 2024), do not scale with zoom, and `required`/`pattern` alone do not tell users the rule in text. Use `novalidate` and your own validation with visible messages, and state the required marker and format in the label or instructions. The author also states a rule against placing error messages under fields (see section 7).

text: Expose field errors with `aria-invalid="true"` (set only after the user interacted or submitted, remove when valid) and associate the message with `aria-describedby`; a polite live region may announce on blur, an assertive one clips the next field's name. `aria-errormessage` is poorly supported (not announced when focusing or on blur); `aria-describedby` is announced consistently when navigating by field, with Chromium treating it as live (JAWS may read it twice). Expect VoiceOver on macOS and iPadOS to differ. Test with the pairings that matter.

text: Name controls in this order: native HTML (`<label for>` with a separate `id`, not an implicit wrapping label, because Dragon and Voice Control do not recognise wrapped labels), then `aria-labelledby` pointing at visible text (can join several ids to make unique names, e.g. in table cells), then visibly-hidden text (use the modern `.visually-hidden` clip pattern, not off-screen positioning), and `aria-label` last. `aria-label` is invisible to voice control, does not enlarge the hit area, is poorly auto-translated and overrides visible text in about a third of real-world uses; `aria-labelledby` overrides a `<label>`. Context may justify exceptions.

text: Do not rely on `<abbr title>` (or `title` in general) to explain abbreviations; exposure differs by browser, screen reader, touch, keyboard and voice access. Expand the term in text on first use, then use the short form.

text: Never rely on the browser default focus ring; it vanishes against same-hue backgrounds (measured 1.02:1 to 1.8:1 in real sites) and textured backgrounds. Supply your own focus style with at least 3:1 contrast against the adjacent colours, test it on every surface colour (dark sections, brand blue buttons) and keep it visible in Windows High Contrast.

applies: all backgrounds, especially coloured CTAs and dark sections.

text: Let users enlarge text at least 200% without loss of content or function (use `rem`, flexible containers; do not lock zoom).

text: Use these width breakpoints for adaptive web and app layouts: compact below 600, medium 600 to 839, expanded 840 to 1199, large 1200 to 1599, extra-large 1600 and above (CSS px). Height classes (compact below 480, medium 480 to 899, expanded 900 and above) matter only for phones in landscape or foldables.
why: Each class is the majority case for a device family (compact: 99.96 percent of portrait phones; medium: 93.73 percent of portrait tablets; expanded: 97.22 percent of landscape tablets), and they map to Material's layout guidance.

text: When stepping up a breakpoint, ask five questions in order: what should be revealed (a rail open by default, a second pane); how should the screen be divided; what should be resized (cards, feeds, lists, panes, with type and margins adjusted); what should be repositioned (actions from bottom to leading edge, a second column, more negative space); what should be swapped (bottom bar to rail). Additional space is not just the same thing bigger.
why: A systematic checklist prevents stretched mobile layouts on desktop.
check: at each breakpoint, the screenshot differs structurally from the previous (a new pane, a swapped component or a repositioned control), not only in scale.

text: Use tone (HCT tone, which equals CIE L*) as the contrast control: in the library's own comment, a tone difference of 40 gives a contrast ratio of at least 3.0 and a difference of 50 gives at least 4.5. Compute the foreground and background L* and require the difference.
why: L* is perceptually linear, so contrast becomes a subtraction; fixed tone gaps make accessible pairs by construction.
check: compute L* = 116 f(Y) - 16 for each text/background pair; require |ΔL*| at least 50 for body text and at least 40 for large text/graphics, then confirm with the actual WCAG ratio. Caveat [computed]: the 50-gap claim holds from about 4.48 to 5.73 depending on position (50 against 100 gives 4.48, just under 4.5) and 40-gap pairs range from 3.17 to 4.15, so always verify the real ratio near the extremes.

text: Treat the colour model as three independent axes: hue 0 to 360 (circular), chroma from 0 (gray) to a hue- and tone-dependent maximum (HCT values top out at roughly 120), tone 0 (black) to 100 (white). Changing hue or chroma at constant tone does not change contrast. Expect chroma to drop when a requested hue/tone cannot render that chroma.
why: Unlike HSL or RGB, HCT lets you move hue and chroma without moving lightness.
check: when generating ramps keep L* constant per step across hues (variance of L* per step below 1); clamp chroma by gamut rather than clipping channels.

text: Set an interaction latency budget: treat 100 ms as the maximum and aim for under 50 ms; for rendering a new thread aim for one or two frames (under 32 ms). Measure everything you want to make fast; cache locally, preload and prerender what is likely next; keep animation minimal; offer keyboard shortcuts with in-UI hints and a command palette (⌘K).
why: Superhuman builds speed as a product feature; the vendor cites older third-party figures for latency cost.
check: measure input-to-visual-response time on core actions (INP below 100 ms; 50 ms target); `performance.measure` marks on key interactions.

text: Start with user needs: research, analyse data, talk to users; do not assume, and remember that what users ask for is not always what they need.
why: Building without needs means building the wrong thing.
check: process: brief states the user need and evidence before visual design.

text: Do the hard work to make it simple: simplicity of use matters more than the look of simplicity; reject "it has always been that way".
why: Making something look simple is easy; making it simple to use means removing underlying complexity.
check: count of steps, fields, and decisions per task versus the previous version (should go down).

text: Iterate: release small, test with real users, add what works, delete what does not, and be willing to scrap a failing prototype.
why: Iteration reduces risk and turns failures into lessons.
check: process: at least one tested iteration recorded in evals.

text: Treat accessibility as part of good design: be inclusive, legible and readable even if it costs elegance; design for needs, not audiences.
why: Those who most need a service often find it hardest to use.
check: run the a11y checklist (A11Y-xx) on every page.

text: Understand the context of use (library, phone, first-time web user) and design for people, not for a screen; build services, not just pages.
why: Context drives constraints (small screen, bad connection, stress).
check: brief names the usage context and device; test at 375 px with throttled network.

text: Be consistent, not uniform: reuse the same language and patterns; deviate only when research says it is better, then share why.
why: Familiarity lowers effort, but a rule book must not freeze improvement.
check: the same action has the same label and component across the product (grep repeated verbs: "Continue" vs "Next").

text: Do less: reuse and link rather than rebuilding; keep to the irreducible core; and minimise environmental impact (principle 11, added 2 April 2025).
why: Less to build, run, and carry.
check: page weight and request counts versus budget; remove features without evidence.

text: Ask one question per page by default; put the question in the `<label>` or `<legend>` and make that the page heading (`<h1>`) so screen readers hear it once. When asking several related things, use a statement heading instead and style each label or legend for scanning.
why: Focus on the specific question and one hearing for screen-reader users.
check: on single-question pages: `h1` is inside `label` or `legend`; on multi-question pages `h1` is a statement and not inside a label or legend.
origin: web:https://design-system.service.gov.uk/

text: Every question page has a back link, a page heading and a "Continue" button; the button is labelled "Continue" (not "Next") and aligned to the left edge of the form.
why: Users do not trust browser back; the left-aligned primary action is not missed.
check: page has `a.back-link` before `main`, one `h1`, and a `button` with text "Continue" whose left edge equals the form column's left edge.
source: patterns/question-pages/ > How it works, Back link, Continue button; components/button.

text: Do not break the browser Back button: Back returns to the previous page in the state the user saw. Exception: after one-time actions such as payment, show a sensible message instead of letting the action repeat.
why: Predictability and safety.
check: step through a flow, press Back: values restored, no duplicate submit.

text: Only ask for information you need and only once per journey; pre-populate or offer carried-forward answers instead of re-asking. Allow "I do not know" where valid.
why: Each field costs completion.
check: audit duplicate field names across steps (same `autocomplete` token twice in one journey = flag).

origin: web:https://design-system.service.gov.uk/

text: Mark optional fields with "(optional)" in the label (or legend for radios and checkboxes); never mark mandatory fields with asterisks.
why: Most fields are required, so flagging the exceptions is quieter and clearer.
check: no `*` in label text; optional inputs have "(optional)" in the label.
source: patterns/question-pages/ > When to use this pattern.
origin: web:https://design-system.service.gov.uk/

text: Use a progress indicator only if testing shows the form is still hard without one; use a simple "Question X of Y" style and only include the total if it is reliable. Avoid the stepper that shows all steps, lets you jump back, and marks the current one.
why: That stepper is often unnoticed, takes space, scales poorly on mobile and is hard to label (one team removed a 12-step indicator with no effect on completion).
check: step-indicator element lists <= 1 step label (current) or a "Step X of Y" text.

text: Avoid range sliders; if used, provide a non-drag way to choose a value.
why: Hard to use for some people; WCAG 2.5.1 Pointer Gestures.
check: every `input[type=range]` has an accompanying number input or buttons.

text: Every text input has a visible label placed above the input, short and direct, in sentence case, without a trailing colon.
why: A persistent label is read reliably by all users.
check: `label` is a block above its `input` (label bottom <= input top); label text does not end in `:`.

text: Do not use placeholder text for labels, hints or examples.
why: It vanishes when typing (a problem for memory conditions and review), some screen readers skip it, and default placeholder colours often fail contrast.
check: `input[placeholder]` count 0 where the label is missing; if a placeholder is present, contrast >= 4.5:1.

text: Hint text is a single short sentence without a full stop, for help most users need, contains no links, and is attached to the input via `aria-describedby`. For long explanation use body content above a specific question label instead of a hint.
why: Screen readers read the whole hint on every focus; links in hints are not announced as links.
check: `.hint` length < 100 characters, does not end with `.`, contains no `a`; has an id referenced by the input's `aria-describedby`.

text: Size inputs to the expected content: fixed-width inputs for known lengths (postcode, phone) and fluid-width classes (full, three-quarters, two-thirds, half, third, quarter) otherwise; fixed widths are sized for 20, 10, 5, 4, 3 and 2 characters.
why: Width signals the expected answer length.

text: For whole numbers use `type="text"` with `inputmode="numeric"`; for decimals use `inputmode="decimal"`; avoid `input type="number"`; for negative numbers use plain text input without `inputmode`.
why: `type=number` allows scroll-wheel increments and gives no feedback on bad input; some mobile keypads cannot enter negatives.

text: For long codes or sequences the user will not have memorised, style the text to separate characters (letter spacing); not needed for phone numbers or postcodes.
why: Helps visual checking.

text: Pick the control by what the toggle means. A checkbox suits on/off data that is submitted with a form and not mistaken for a choice; a `button` with `aria-pressed` (or `role=switch` with `aria-checked`) suits an immediate-effect toggle; radio pair inside `fieldset`/`legend` suits an explicit on/off choice. Do not use links for toggles.
why: Checkboxes and radios read as data inputs; buttons are the expected element for in-interface state changes.

text: A toggle button is `<button type="button">` with `aria-pressed` set to an explicit `"true"` or `"false"` at all times; the absence of the attribute means "not a toggle". `type="button"` stops accidental form submission.
why: ARIA state attributes are strings; a missing attribute loses the state announcement.

text: A toggletip (click-triggered info bubble, usually an "i") is a `<button type="button">` plus an empty live region (`role="status"`) in the DOM beforehand. On click, clear the region, then after a short delay (about 100 ms) insert the bubble text; close on Esc, blur or outside click. Do not use `aria-describedby` for the bubble content.

text: Do not build tabs unless the use case benefits. A table of contents with same-page links, or an accordion, is simpler and more robust. Do not style a link list as tabs, and never use tab styling or tab semantics for site-wide navigation or router views.

text: A real tab interface: container `role="tablist"`; each tab `role="tab"` with `aria-selected`; each panel `role="tabpanel"` with `aria-labelledby` pointing at its tab; inactive panels hidden; selected tab has `tabindex` default (0) while others have `tabindex="-1"`; Left/Right arrows move and activate tabs; Tab moves into the active panel; Shift+Tab returns to the selected tab. text: For single-page-app views use real links, then move focus to the new view's heading (`tabindex="-1"`) or labelled region and update `<title>` to `App | View`. Do not mark views as tabpanels.

text: When tabs do not fit, collapse the tab list into a single column of options (selected one clearly marked) rather than converting to an accordion; if the number of tabs is unknown or large, use an accordion at all widths.

text: Put a real ``), not `role=button` on the heading, and not a click handler on the heading. Reset button styles with `all: inherit` and restore a focus style.

text: Offer expand-all and collapse-all as two separate buttons inside a labelled list (`ul aria-label`), never one toggle, because sections can be in mixed states.

text: If a URL hash targets a collapsed section, open it and focus its button on load, and update the hash when the user opens a section so links are shareable.

text: An application menu button (true menu): `button[aria-haspopup][aria-expanded]` opens `role="menu"` containing `menuitem` (or `menuitemradio`/`menuitemcheckbox` with `aria-checked`), items `tabindex="-1"`. text: Only tabular data goes in `table`. Header cells are `th` (`scope="col"` or `scope="row"` for row headers), every table has a `caption` (headings may sit inside it) or an immediately preceding heading, and avoid the deprecated `summary`. Within a `figure` a `figcaption` serves.

text: A slider should never move without a user action: no auto-advance, no timers. Movement is by scrolling, swipe, arrow keys or buttons only.

text: Elements that behave alike must look alike (colour, shape, size, orientation); elements that behave differently must differ. In particular, links and nav items must be visually distinguishable from body text.

text: Prefer the simplest shape or figure that conveys the meaning; reduce illustrations, icons and layouts to one clear overall form rather than many competing parts.
